title: When Algorithms Decide Your Career: AI Hiring Under Fire
excerpt: A landmark lawsuit against Workday and a wave of new state laws are forcing a reckoning over AI tools that screen, rank, and reject millions of workers.
body:
A federal court ruling, new state regulations, and a growing stack of lawsuits are converging to make AI-driven hiring one of the defining legal battlegrounds of 2025 — and the rules of the game are shifting fast.

**What happened — the Workday case goes national:**
On May 16, 2025, Judge Rita Lin of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California certified a nationwide collective action against HR software giant Workday, allowing millions of job seekers over age 40 to join the suit. The plaintiffs allege that Workday's AI screening tools systematically disqualify applicants based on age, race, and disability. In court filings, Workday itself acknowledged that '1.1 billion applications were rejected' using its software tools during the relevant period — making this potentially one of the largest discrimination collectives ever assembled.

**Why it matters — a patchwork of state laws fills the federal void:**
With the Trump administration's January 2025 executive order rolling back federal AI oversight — and the EEOC quietly removing its own AI hiring guidance from its website — states are charging ahead. California's new Civil Rights Council regulations, effective October 1, 2025, make it unlawful to use any automated-decision system that discriminates based on protected traits, and mandate *meaningful human oversight* over every AI hiring tool. Illinois, Colorado, and Texas have each passed or enacted their own AI employment laws, creating a patchwork that employers must now navigate alone. AI training data that reflects historical inequities — such as eras when women or minorities were routinely passed over — teaches these systems to replicate those exact patterns.

**What to watch — litigation and legislation accelerate:**
As the Workday case heads toward discovery and class notification, every employer using algorithmic screening tools faces mounting legal exposure — and the next wave of lawsuits against the companies that *use* these tools, not just the vendors, is widely expected to follow.
